topics.title: Thomson's model and the gold foil experiment

learn.hook: Imagine firing cannon shells at a sheet of tissue paper and seeing a few bounce straight back. That was Rutherford's astonishment at the gold foil results.
points: Atoms are electrically neutral, and each element gives a characteristic spectrum. A good atomic model must explain both structure and spectra.
Thomson's 'plum pudding' model (1898): positive charge spread uniformly through the atom, with electrons embedded like seeds in a watermelon. It could not explain large-angle scattering.

Geiger-Marsden experiment (1911, suggested by Rutherford): a beam of alpha particles was aimed at a very thin gold foil; scattered particles were detected by flashes on a zinc sulphide (ZnS) screen viewed through a microscope.
Observations: most alpha particles passed straight through; a few were deflected through large angles; a very few (about 1 in 8000) were turned back by more than 90°.
Conclusion: the atom's positive charge and nearly all its mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, about 10⁴ to 10⁵ times smaller than the atom; most of the atom is empty space.

example.q: Why did most alpha particles pass undeflected through the gold foil?
steps: The nucleus occupies a tiny fraction of the atom's volume.
Most of the atom is empty space.
Most alpha particles never come close to a nucleus.
example.answer: Because most of the atom is empty space

learn.reallife: Students at Indian science festivals often recreate the Rutherford experiment with marbles rolled at a hidden central block: most roll past, a few bounce sharply off.

topics.title: Impact parameter and distance of closest approach

learn.hook: How close can an alpha particle get to a gold nucleus before it is turned back? Energy conservation gives a surprisingly simple estimate of nuclear size.
points: The path of an alpha particle near a nucleus depends on its impact parameter b: the perpendicular distance of its initial line of motion from the nucleus.
Small b (nearly head-on) gives large scattering angles; b = 0 means the particle turns back (scattering through 180°). Large b gives little deflection.
In a head-on approach, the alpha particle stops momentarily at the distance of closest approach d, where all its kinetic energy has become electric potential energy.
K = (1/4πε₀)(2e)(Ze)/d, so d = (1/4πε₀)(2Ze²)/K.
d gives an upper limit for the nuclear size; for gold and alpha energies of a few MeV, d is a few × 10⁻¹⁴ m.

example.q: An alpha particle of 7.2 MeV heads straight for a tin nucleus (Z = 50). Find the distance of closest approach. (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

learn.reallife: Particle accelerators like the Pelletron at TIFR Mumbai fire nuclei at targets; physicists use closest-approach estimates to judge whether nuclei will touch and react.

topics.title: Electron orbits and the trouble with Rutherford's model

learn.hook: Rutherford's atom was a mini solar system. But classical physics predicted that it should collapse in a split second. Clearly, something was missing.
points: In Rutherford's planetary model, the electron orbits the nucleus with the Coulomb attraction providing centripetal force: mv²/r = e²/(4πε₀r²).
Kinetic energy K = e²/(8πε₀r), potential energy U = -e²/(4πε₀r), total energy E = K + U = -e²/(8πε₀r).
The total energy is negative, meaning the electron is bound to the nucleus. Energy must be supplied to free it.
Limitation 1: an orbiting electron accelerates, and by classical EM theory it should radiate energy continuously, spiralling into the nucleus. Atoms would be unstable.
Limitation 2: a spiralling electron would emit a continuous range of frequencies, but atoms emit sharp line spectra.

example.q: For a hydrogen electron orbit, K = 13.6 eV. Find U and the total energy E.

learn.reallife: Fluorescent tube lights and sodium-vapour street lamps along Indian highways glow in definite colours, line spectra that Rutherford's model could not explain.

learn.hook: Astronomers know what distant stars are made of without ever visiting them. Each element leaves a unique barcode of light.
points: When a gas or vapour is excited (for example by an electric discharge or heating), it emits light only at certain wavelengths: an emission line spectrum of bright lines on a dark background.
Each element has its own characteristic set of lines.
When white light passes through a cool gas, the gas absorbs light at the same wavelengths it would emit, giving dark lines on a continuous background: an absorption spectrum.
The emission and absorption lines of an element appear at the same wavelengths.
Because spectra are unique, they act as fingerprints for identifying elements in labs, in industry and in stars (helium was first discovered in the Sun's spectrum).

example.q: Sodium vapour gives a bright yellow emission line near 589 nm. Where will a dark line appear if white light passes through cool sodium vapour?
steps: Absorption lines lie at the same wavelengths as emission lines.

learn.reallife: Forensic and food-testing labs in India, including those under FSSAI, use atomic absorption spectroscopy to detect metals like lead in food and water.

learn.hook: In 1913 Niels Bohr rescued the nuclear atom by making three bold rules. They broke classical physics but matched the hydrogen spectrum beautifully.
points: Postulate 1: electrons revolve in certain stable orbits (stationary states) without radiating energy.
Postulate 2: in these orbits, angular momentum is quantised: L = mvr = nh/2π, where n = 1, 2, 3, ... is the principal quantum number.
Postulate 3: an electron emits or absorbs a photon only when it jumps between orbits: hν = Ei - Ef.
Radius of the nth orbit: rn = n²h²ε₀/(πme²), so rn ∝ n². The smallest, the Bohr radius, is a₀ ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m (0.53 Å).
Speed of the electron in the nth orbit vn ∝ 1/n; in the first orbit v₁ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (about c/137).

example.q: Find the radius of the third orbit of hydrogen and the electron's speed there, compared with the first orbit.
example.answer: r₃ = 4.77 Å; speed is one third of the first orbit's

learn.reallife: Astronomers at Indian observatories such as Hanle and Devasthal still label hydrogen lines by Bohr's quantum numbers (for example the n = 3 to n = 2 line), and his model is the first quantum atom taught in every CBSE Class 12 classroom.

learn.hook: An electron in hydrogen lives on an energy staircase. The bottom step is at -13.6 eV, and the steps crowd together as they climb towards zero.
points: Energy of the nth level of hydrogen: En = -13.6/n² eV. E₁ = -13.6 eV, E₂ = -3.4 eV, E₃ = -1.51 eV, E₄ = -0.85 eV, ... up to E∞ = 0.
n = 1 is the ground state; n ≥ 2 are excited states. The energy level diagram shows levels getting closer together as n increases.
Ionisation energy of hydrogen from the ground state = 13.6 eV. Excitation energy from n = 1 to n = 2 = 10.2 eV.
Energy needed to ionise from level n is 13.6/n² eV. Above E = 0 the electron is free and can have any (continuous) energy.
The Franck-Hertz experiment (1914) gave direct evidence for discrete energy levels: electrons colliding with mercury atoms lost energy only in definite amounts.

example.q: How much energy is needed to ionise a hydrogen atom from the n = 3 state?

learn.reallife: The plasma physicists at the Institute for Plasma Research, Gandhinagar, study hydrogen at temperatures where atoms are ionised, i.e. electrons have been pushed above the E = 0 level.

learn.hook: Every line in the hydrogen spectrum is an electron jumping down the energy staircase and throwing off a photon whose energy matches the drop.
points: A spectral line arises when an electron jumps from a higher level ni to a lower level nf, emitting a photon of energy hν = Ei - Ef.
ν = (13.6 eV/h)(1/nf² - 1/ni²), or 1/λ = R(1/nf² - 1/ni²), where R ≈ 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ is the Rydberg constant.
Absorption lines correspond to the same energy differences in reverse (nf → ni upward).
A transition from n = 3 to n = 2 gives a red line near 656 nm; transitions ending on n = 1 give ultraviolet lines.
Handy shortcut: λ (in nm) = 1240/ΔE (in eV).

learn.reallife: The pink-red glow of hydrogen in nebulae photographed by Indian astronomers at Hanle, Ladakh, comes from the n = 3 to n = 2 transition.

topics.title: Bohr's orbits as matter waves, and limits of the model

learn.hook: Why should angular momentum come in multiples of h/2π? A decade after Bohr, de Broglie's matter waves gave a beautiful answer.
points: de Broglie's explanation: an electron in a Bohr orbit is a standing wave, like a vibrating string closed into a circle.
For a stable standing wave, the circumference must hold a whole number of wavelengths: 2πr = nλ.
With λ = h/(mv): 2πr = nh/(mv), so mvr = nh/2π, exactly Bohr's quantisation condition.

Limitations of Bohr's model: it works only for hydrogen-like atoms (one electron, such as He⁺ and Li²⁺); it cannot explain the relative intensities of spectral lines or the spectra of many-electron atoms.
Problem toolkit: rn ∝ n², vn ∝ 1/n, En ∝ -1/n²; number of spectral lines from level n down to ground state = n(n - 1)/2.

example.q: An electron in hydrogen is excited to n = 4. How many different spectral lines can be emitted as it returns to the ground state?

learn.reallife: Guitar and sitar strings vibrate only at frequencies that fit whole numbers of half-wavelengths on them; de Broglie pictured electrons in atoms the same way.
